query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their mechanical and thermoelastic behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In refractory high-entropy alloys, the inherent compositional complexity leads to heterogeneous lattice strain that promotes the formation of non‐traditional dislocation structures (such as multiple kinks/jogs and bidirectional cross slips). This stabilized dislocation behavior enhances strength retention and thermoelastic performance at high temperatures compared to conventional refractory alloys with less lattice distortion.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloys (e.g., NbTaTiVZr or similar compositions) prepared in an as-synthesized state with pronounced compositional complexity and inherent lattice strain.
generation.intervention: Perform a controlled comparison by synthesizing two sets of alloys: one RHEA with high compositional complexity (thus large lattice distortion) and a baseline conventional refractory alloy (or a modified HEA with reduced compositional disorder) exhibiting minimal lattice strain.
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions (T ≥ 1000 °C) under mechanical loading (tensile or compressive tests) with identical processing and heat treatment protocols to isolate the effect of lattice distortion.
generation.structural_mediator: Heterogeneous lattice strain that encourages the stabilization of dislocation substructures (multiple kinks/jogs and enhanced cross-slip activity).
generation.mechanism: The localized lattice distortions create internal stress fields that modify the dislocation core structures. This alteration reduces dislocation mobility in a controlled manner, thereby increasing the material's strength and influencing its thermoelastic response by limiting the extension of the plastic zone during deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the conventional refractory alloy, the RHEA with higher lattice distortion should exhibit: (1) a higher strength retention at elevated temperatures; (2) distinct dislocation features observable via in-situ TEM (e.g., multiple kinks/jogs and increased cross-slip events); and (3) altered thermoelastic properties such as modified elastic moduli and thermal expansion behavior.
generation.baseline: Conventional refractory alloys or modified HEAs with intentionally reduced compositional complexity (and hence lower lattice distortion) subjected to the same high-temperature mechanical tests.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable under high-temperature service conditions (≥ 1000 °C) and may not predict behavior accurately at room temperature or under very different loading regimes. The specific contribution of compositional electronic effects versus lattice distortion is not addressed and remains outside the scope.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the quantitative extent to which lattice distortion, as opposed to other alloying effects (such as electronic contributions), governs the observed mechanical and thermoelastic behavior. Variations in processing conditions and exact compositions may also modify the relative contributions of the proposed mechanism.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two series of alloys: (A) a high-entropy alloy with high compositional complexity to induce large lattice distortions and (B) a conventional refractory alloy or an HEA modified to have reduced lattice distortion. Subject both series to identical high-temperature mechanical (tensile/compression) tests and perform in-situ TEM to document dislocation behavior during deformation.
measurements: Mechanical strength and plastic strain response at T ≥ 1000 °C
Thermoelastic parameters (elastic moduli, thermal expansion coefficients)
Direct TEM imaging of dislocation structures (e.g., presence of multiple kinks, jogs, cross-slip patterns)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy (group A) does not exhibit statistically significant differences in dislocation structures, strength retention, or thermoelastic behavior relative to the baseline alloy (group B), then the proposed role of heterogeneous lattice strain as the governing mechanism would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractIn order to find more excellent structural materials resistant to radiation damage, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have been developed due to their characteristics of limited point defect diffusion such as lattice distortion and slow diffusion. Specially, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) that can adapt to a high-temperature environment are badly needed. In this study, TiZrHfNbMo0.1 RHEAs are selected for irradiation and nanoindentation experiments. We combined the mechanistic model for the depth-dependent hardness of ion-irradiated metals and the introduction of the scale factor f to modify the irradiation-hardening model in order to better describe the nanoindentation indentation process in the irradiated layer. Finally, it can be found that, with the increase in irradiation dose, a more serious lattice distortion caused by a higher defect density limits the expansion of the plastic zone.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, mechanical properties, ion irradiation, indentation size effect, plastic zone

Our results reveal that the heterogeneous lattice strain causes unusual dislocation behaviors (i.e., multiple kinks/jogs and bidirectional cross slips), resulting in the strengthening mechanisms that underpin the strength-ductility synergy. The outcome of our research sheds important insights into the design of strong yet ductile distorted crystalline solids, such as high-entropy alloys and high-entropy ceramics.
